visual_base.visual_narrative_log: (1) A middle-aged man with short black hair and glasses is positioned in the center of the frame, wearing a formal black button-down shirt. He stands in a professional studio environment featuring a dark gray curtain backdrop and a wooden bookshelf on the left side, which holds several books and small decorative items. He actively uses his hands to gesture as he speaks directly to the camera. The lighting is bright and even, highlighting his facial expressions and the texture of his shirt against the darker background. (2) A sharp cut transitions to a visual overlay showing a real-world concrete levee situated along a brown, slow-moving river under a bright, partly cloudy sky. The man remains in the background, though partially obscured by the large rectangular image of the infrastructure. The levee is curved and made of modern, light-gray poured concrete, contrasting with the natural muddy water and the greenery on the opposite bank. (3) A digital technical diagram is presented, illustrating a river channel with teal-colored water. It features a specific 'open levee' or 'Kaiko-tei' design where the defense walls overlap but leave a gap. Blue arrows indicate the primary flow of the river, while additional arrows show how overflow is directed into a drainage or buffer area. (4) The scene shifts to a montage of comparisons, including a photo of a medieval stone castle wall with distinct square notches or crenellations, followed by a humorous cartoon graphic of a large, smiling meat bun (baozi). The man in the studio continues to speak, his hands moving rhythmically to emphasize the differences between these items and the actual engineering concept. (5) A detailed high-angle shot showcases a physical terrain model on a table. The model includes a blue-painted river path, green textured grass, and miniature white houses with black roofs representing a village. The 'open levee' structure is clearly modeled with overlapping physical barriers, demonstrating how water would naturally enter the designated flood-retention areas during a surge. (6) Historical visual evidence is introduced, including a traditional portrait of a Japanese lord, Takeda Shingen, and photos of 'Seigyu' or wooden tripod river defenses. These images are displayed as large rectangular overlays while the narrator explains the historical origins of the technique. (7) A cinematic clip from a movie shows a man frustrated inside a car during a heavy traffic jam, used as a metaphor for river congestion. This is followed by shots of parched, cracked earth and a person in a blue shirt striking a large stone wall with a sledgehammer, visually representing the destructive force of water and the failure of rigid defenses.
